issue_context.title: Rate limit of mount events makes starting/stopping mount units unreliable
issue_context.body:
**systemd version the issue has been seen with**
248.5 and 248.6, not 248.3

<!-- **NOTE:** Do not submit bug reports about anything but the two most recently released *major* systemd versions upstream! -->
<!--           If there have been multiple stable releases for that major version, please consider updating to a recent one before reporting an issue. -->
<!--           When using a distro package, please make sure that the version reported is meaningful for upstream. -->
<!-- See https://github.com/systemd/systemd-stable/releases for the list of most recent releases. -->
<!-- For older version please use distribution trackers (see https://systemd.io/CONTRIBUTING#filing-issues). -->

**Used distribution**
 > openSUSE Tumbleweed

**Linux kernel version used** (`uname -a`)
<!-- Make sure to enclose the pasted kernel version in `backticks`, so that
     GitHub doesn't convert the `#` character typically included in it into a
     reference to old GitHub issues. -->
 > `Linux d142 5.13.4-1-default #1 SMP Thu Jul 22 15:55:06 UTC 2021 (91a0cca) x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux`

**CPU architecture issue was seen on**
 > x86_64

**Unexpected behaviour you saw**
 > After a batch of (un)mount events which trigger the sd-event rate limit, starting/stopping of (unrelated) `.mount` units becomes unreliable.
> Doing a `umount` followed by a `systemctl start` of the `.mount` unit is successful, but the mount didn't actually happen.
> Doing a `mount` followed by a `systemctl stop` of the `.mount` unit is successful, but the mount is still there.

**Steps to reproduce the problem**
This is a somewhat artificial test. In a real system, this is triggered by setup and teardown of a `chroot` environment, which breaks other services running shortly after it.

```
echo 'tmpfs /mnt tmpfs defaults,nofail 0 0' >> /etc/fstab
systemctl daemon-reload
mkdir -p foo
systemctl start mnt.mount

for ((i=0;i<50;++i)); do mount --bind foo foo; umount foo; done; # Trigger rate limit
umount /mnt; systemctl start mnt.mount; echo $?; mountpoint /mnt; systemctl status mnt.mount; mountpoint /mnt
```

It's expected that after `umount /mnt; systemctl start mnt.mount`, the `mnt.mount` unit is active and `/mnt` mounted. What actually happens is that the `systemctl start mnt.mount` effectively does nothing: The `mnt.mount` unit is (still) up, but `/mnt` is not mounted:

```
0
/mnt is not a mountpoint
● mnt.mount - /mnt
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/fstab; generated)
     Active: active (mounted) since Wed 2021-07-28 09:36:10 UTC; 4s ago
      Where: /mnt
       What: tmpfs
       Docs: man:fstab(5)
             man:systemd-fstab-generator(8)
      Tasks: 0 (limit: 4660)
        CPU: 5ms
     CGroup: /system.slice/mnt.mount
/mnt is not a mountpoint
```

There's a clear "happens-before" relationship of `umount` and `systemctl start`, so I would not expect any race condition.

**Additional program output to the terminal or log subsystem illustrating the issue**

<!-- Please paste relevant program terminal or journal output here, ideally
     when generated in debug mode (try setting the SYSTEMD_LOG_LEVEL=debug
     environment variable). For very long copy/pasted data consider using a
     service like https://gist.github.com/. Where copy/paste is not possible
     (for example early boot or late shutdown), a photo of the screen might do
     too, but text is always much preferred. -->

Because of the rate limit, the unmount event of `/mnt` is processed after the request to `start mnt.mount`, so at that point systemd believes that the mount is still active and it doesn't actually do the mount. It looks like this in the debug log:

```text
Event source 0x561313e8ad70 (mount-monitor-dispatch) entered rate limit state.
...
mnt.mount: Trying to enqueue job mnt.mount/start/replace
mnt.mount: Installed new job mnt.mount/start as 985
mnt.mount: Enqueued job mnt.mount/start as 985
...
mnt.mount: Job 985 mnt.mount/start finished, result=done
...
Event source 0x561313e8ad70 (mount-monitor-dispatch) left rate limit state.
mnt.mount: Deactivated successfully.
mnt.mount: Changed mounted -> dead
mnt.mount: Consumed 4ms CPU time.
```

What could be done is to force processing of all mount events in the queue whenever a `.mount` unit is queried or changed. That approach should not conflict with #15464.

A workaround is to never mix `systemctl start/stop .mount` and `mount/umount`.

Isn't this the usual problem with /proc/mountinfo being racy and generally a terrible interface for anything besides the simplest use cases? What happened to the mount notifications and fsinfo() patch series? /cc @brauner

> Isn't this the usual problem with /proc/mountinfo being racy and generally a terrible interface for anything besides the simplest use cases? What happened to the mount notifications and fsinfo() patch series? /cc @brauner

It died because of Red Hat internal disagreements what this interface should really look like ending in a shouting match and the patch got abandoned. Though David still intends to work on it. I'll chat to him about it soon.

> > Isn't this the usual problem with /proc/mountinfo being racy and generally a terrible interface for anything besides the simplest use cases? What happened to the mount notifications and fsinfo() patch series? /cc @brauner
> 
> It died because of Red Hat internal disagreements what this interface should really look like ending in a shouting match and the patch got abandoned. Though David still intends to work on it. I'll chat to him about it soon.

This is completely wrong, there was a lot of development and many changes along the way but there weren't internal disagreements preventing it from being merged, at least not within RedHat as far as I know.

You must be referring to Miklos Szeredi not liking the fsinfo() interface which was unfortunate and IMHO missed the point of what the fsinfo() system call was meant to do. His upstream comments were based only on the mount table info. case and it was an upstream discussion, I don't remember us discussing that internally with Miklos (also see below the comment about the design being different to the usual approach).

The problem ended up being the fsinfo() system call, the notifications series would probably have been merged and I think it was partly merged but, for the mount table use case, that's not enough the fsinfo() call is also needed.

Linus wanted people that would use the fsinfo() system call and had code ready to go to speak up (kind of unrealistic since those people are probably not reading the LKML or fsdevel mailing lists, but that's the way it was).

Karl Zak and I had been working on code for libmount and I was well along with code for systemd but that wasn't enough for Linus.

The fsinfo() system call has a much larger scope because it is meant to provide a wide range of information about file systems and allow file systems to customize that information if the filesystem needed to do so.

The fsinfo() system call wasn't just about providing mount table information in an efficient way, it was much more than that.

And the implementation design was different to what is normally used in the kernel, which is another reason for the reluctance, hence the need to prove it would be used.

In the end we couldn't get enough buy in from a sufficient number of potential users to speak up so Linus wouldn't merge the fsinfo() changes.

AFAIK David did need those fsinfo() changes so cutting it down didn't make sense, which is still a problem.

Unless we can get sufficient buy in from others that would use this change, for other than the mount table case, then we are stuck.

Thanks for the update, very interesting. Any reason why the mount table use case is not enough by itself? I mean we'd use it here without any doubt, this is one of the most long standing and unsolvable issues we have - using mounts at scale and reliably is factually impossible without those kernel changes. Isn't this enough for merging? What other users or use cases should speak up?

I guess that's part of the problem, I don't know what David had in mind or who was asking for it so I couldn't ask people to join in myself. I can see the utility of what was being provided though.

There was a lot of duplication of information provided by existing system calls and a lot of extended information too.
And there's ongoing support, at one time Al said he didn't like the way it was extendible saying it would end up a maintenance headache.

Anyway it ended up Linus essentially saying who's going to use "all" this and not getting the answers he wanted, I believe he wasn't convinced the existing proc mount table handling was as serious a problem as it is in spite of the performance improvements for mount handling (I'm pretty sure I described my findings, it was a while ago). But he did say he got the need for the notifications improvements.

Unfortunately without a relatively low overhead way to get the extra information about a given mount directly the notifications, in particular the event queuing functionality, it isn't really that useful AFAICS.

For my part it is the mount table handling that I need it for too, not so much for autofs itself but for the disruption that can be caused by large mount tables and frequent mount activity due to people using largish autofs configurations. It can play havoc on applications that monitor the mount table, like systemd and udiskd. But it sounds like your no stranger to that.

I'm tempted to bore you with some of the test results but this is already way out of scope for this issue, ;)

Getting back to the problem here though, I always thought that the 1 second quiescence of the rate limiting was way too long.

I wonder if cutting that back to around 250ms would mostly resolve this problem, a sort of a poor mans event queuing facility rather than a let's just ignore these things for a "whole" second to lower overhead. I wonder how much impact that would have on the rate limiting performance improvement too ...

@raven-au from my point of view, David's interface was too complex and with predefined structs. I can imagine a simple fsinfo() interface where userspace defines an array of variables, allocate space for the result and kernel fill the fields by data from VFS; just simple 'key' and 'value' API where one syscall can return multiple values for the mountpoint. This solution will be open for arbitrary new fields and userspace will get who it asks for. I agree that procfs based solution (Mikos' idea?) is odd. It seems better to get so basic information without /proc.

So I think what we should be doing to fix the issue is to make unit_start() for mount units return -EAGAIN when we notice the mount table watching is ratelimited. This should fix the job queue issues, as it means we won't act on mount units unless we also know our current idea of the mount table is up-to-date.

It's probably a very simple fix: implement the existing `test_start_limit()` vtable function for .mount units (it currently is only implemented in service units). There, just return EAGAIN when the rate limit of the /proc/self/mountinfo event source is currently in effect.

(The vtable function should probably be renamed though, since it is used for more that start limits.)

In addition to this, once we leave the rate limiting we should issue  `sd_event_source_set_enabled(j->manager->run_queue_event_source, SD_EVENT_ONESHOT)` once. This ensures the run queue is triggered again, and we try to find runnable jobs again, which might then succeed given the EAGAIN situation was now corrected.

event_source_leave_ratelimit() is also called by sd_event_source_set_ratelimit() in some cases. I think in that case we really shouldn't invoke the callback though (rule should be: invoke callbacks only when the event loop is run, not when it is configured). i.e. add a boolean or so as parameter to the function that controls whether to call the callbacks or to skip it.

hmm, so, when process_timer() is called and as effect we might call the ratelimit expiry callback I think we should not continue with the processing but immediately go for the next event loop iteration. Specifically:

1. whenever we actually invoke such a callback,  event_source_leave_ratelimit() should return with a return code of 1.
2. whenever process_timer() sees that for any of the event sources it should also return with an exit code of 1 (but call the callback for all event sources where it is defined)
3. whenever sd_event_wait() sees that it should (after all other event sources have been process) put the event loop into INITIAL state and return 0, rather than PENDING state and return 1.

Why? because the ratelimit expiry callbacks likely reenable event sources, and if they did so we should first see if there's something pending for them before we actually dispatch a proper IO event or so. sd_event_wait() returns 1 if the caller should call sd_event_dispatch() next (i.e. there's an event source ready to be dispatched), but returns 0 if it should just be called again (i.e. there's nothing to be dispatched). Thus, if one of these expiry callbacks are called we must make sure sd_event_wait() consequently returns 0 so that we then check all IO sources properly again and take any event source that was enabled back into consideration.
